items.name: Restrooms & Accessibility
items.desc: Public restrooms are available around the terminal's waiting and activity areas, usually with accessible stalls and family/changing rooms. Main entrances and walkways are generally barrier-free.
items.tip: On busy ship days crowds grow quickly, so use the facilities closest to your gangway.

items.name: Parking & Shuttles
items.desc: Parking areas for private cars and tour coaches sit near the terminal, and taxis and shared minibuses (colectivos) run within walking distance to the island's main towns.
items.tip: Many visitors walk to town or take a colectivo instead of renting a car.

items.name: Dining Options
items.desc: The terminal and Coxen Hole offer a range of eateries by type — fast food, cafés, Caribbean restaurants and street-food stalls — for every budget.
items.tip: Small vendors are often cash-only, so carry some local currency; eat well before swimming.

items.name: Lodging Types
items.desc: On-island accommodation comes in many types — resorts, boutique hotels, guesthouses and hostels — mainly around West Bay, West End and local communities.
items.tip: If staying overnight, book a registered property, keep your confirmation, and arrange transfers in advance.

items.name: Shops & Essentials
items.desc: The terminal shopping village, town supermarkets and convenience stores sell souvenirs, drinks, daily essentials and basic medicines.
items.tip: Shop traffic follows the ship schedule; do errands in the morning to avoid the rush.

items.name: Fuel & Charging
items.desc: Fuel stations on Roatán are limited and sit mostly along main roads; some lodgings and public areas offer power outlets for devices.
items.tip: Top up before long drives and carry a power bank and adapter.

items.name: Health & Emergency
items.desc: Coxen Hole has hospitals and clinics; the terminal area usually keeps first-aid and security staff, and town pharmacies stock common medicines.
items.tip: Keep personal medication with you in its labelled container; contact port staff or local emergency services if needed.

items.name: Connectivity
items.desc: Free Wi-Fi is common at the terminal and main public areas, and local carrier stores sell prepaid SIM cards around the island.
items.tip: Check your roaming plan before leaving the ship, or pick up a local SIM to stay connected.

seasonPlan.title: Seasonal Visit Planner
seasonPlan.subtitle: How weather, water and wildlife change through the year around Roatán.
seasonPlan.basedOn: A general guide based on long-term seasonal climate patterns; combine it with the live weather above and any official advisories before you go.

rows.weather: Early dry season: steady trade winds, around 24–29°C, little rain.
rows.water: Sea around 27°C with good visibility; generally calm seas on the north reef.
rows.wildlife: Migratory birds and reef fish are active — good for birdwatching and snorkelling.
rows.advice: Peak international holiday season; book transport and stays well in advance.

rows.weather: Driest part of the year: strong sun, gentle breezes, 26–31°C.
rows.water: Usually the best visibility of the year — the prime window for snorkelling and diving.
rows.wildlife: Coral spawning approaches and whale-shark sightings are relatively common from March to May.
rows.advice: Best months for the water and underwater photography; use sunscreen and hydration, avoid midday heat.

rows.weather: Rainy season begins: sunny spells with short showers, warmest at 27–32°C.
rows.water: After rain the near shore can briefly turn turbid or drift with sargassum; it usually clears quickly.
rows.wildlife: Turtle nesting and hatchling season, with more offshore pelagic activity.
rows.advice: Carry a light rain jacket; plan water activities for the morning, as showers peak in the afternoon.

rows.weather: Peak of the wet season with higher wind and rain, overlapping the Atlantic hurricane season (Sep–Oct).
rows.water: Choppier seas and more variable visibility; watch currents and swell at times.
rows.wildlife: Water quality can vary in some areas, though reefs and fish remain worth seeing — judge on site.
rows.advice: Watch forecasts and port updates, keep a backup plan; fewer crowds and lower prices reward flexible travellers.

stewardship.title: Reef Science & Visitor Responsibility
stewardship.subtitle: Understand a little ocean ecology — your visit becomes easier and the reef lasts longer.
stewardship.scienceTitle: Why this place is special — a quick reef ecology primer

scienceItems.name: Coral reefs: the rainforests of the sea
scienceItems.text: Tiny coral polyps and their symbiotic algae build limestone skeletons that shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species. Roatán is part of the Mesoamerican Reef, the world's second-largest barrier reef system.

scienceItems.name: Seagrass and mangroves as guardians
scienceItems.text: Seagrass beds nurse turtles and juvenile fish while filtering the water; mangroves stabilise shores. Together they complete the lagoon's living chain.

scienceItems.name: Daily life of fish and turtles
scienceItems.text: Parrotfish graze the reef and keep it healthy; hawksbill and green turtles forage year-round near shore. Meet a whale shark? Keep your distance and never chase.

scienceItems.name: An island born of limestone
scienceItems.text: Roatán is a raised limestone island — centuries of erosion shaped the ridges, caves and bays you see today.

dutyItems.name: Do not touch or stand on coral
dutyItems.text: Coral is fragile — one touch can kill a colony. Snorkel with a respectful distance and use your fins for control.

dutyItems.name: Never feed marine life
dutyItems.text: Feeding changes wild behaviour and burdens local waters.

dutyItems.name: Choose reef-friendly sun care
dutyItems.text: Before swimming, limit sunscreens with oxybenzone and similar filters; prefer shade, rash guards and reef-safe products.

dutyItems.name: Carry your rubbish out
dutyItems.text: Use a refillable bottle and reusable bags, avoid single-use plastics, and leave no litter on sand or sea.

dutyItems.name: Do not buy coral or wildlife souvenirs
dutyItems.text: Many 'keepsakes' come from protected waters — take only photos and memories.

dutyItems.name: Follow on-site rules
dutyItems.text: Heed buoys, restricted areas and opening times, and follow lifeguard and port staff instructions.

heritage.title: Stories Behind the Name: From a Pirate Cove to a Modern Cruise Gateway
heritage.subtitle: Background tales and local lore that give Coxen Hole and Mahogany Bay their character.
heritage.note: Compiled for general interest from published local histories and oral tradition; details may vary between sources.

cards.heading: Pirate days and the name 'Coxen Hole'
cards.text: The most popular local account says Coxen Hole takes its name from John Coxen, an English pirate captain active in these waters in the 1600s. What drew him was this sheltered, deep natural bay — his crew is said to have used it as an anchorage, and a hint of that 'pirate harbour' romance survives in the town today.

cards.heading: 1797: the Garifuna sea epic
cards.text: In 1797 a group of Garifuna people, removed from St Vincent, paddled dugout canoes to Roatán — beginning the celebrated chapter of this African-Caribbean people along the Central American coast. Their drums, language and cooking remain a core of Bay Islands culture.

cards.heading: English, Spanish and the change of 1859
cards.text: Before becoming Honduran, the Bay Islands sat under strong British influence, which is why English and Spanish still live side by side. Following treaties signed in 1859, the islands formally joined Honduras as the modern Bay Islands department.

cards.heading: 'Mahogany Bay' and the island's timber memory
cards.text: In the age of sail and colonial trade, mahogany and logwood ranked among Central America's most valuable exports, and timber camps once dotted the island's interior. Locals often link the name Mahogany Bay to that history — whatever its exact origin, it keeps alive a memory of timber and tall ships.

intro.title: About Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal
intro.overview: Welcome to **Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal** — now branded **Isla Tropicale** — Carnival Corporation's private cruise port on Roatán. It sits in the **Dixon Cove** area of the **Bay Islands** department of **Honduras** (Google Maps lists the area as Coxen Hole). This is a separate terminal from the **Port of Roatán** in Coxen Hole town, and serves as the primary gateway for Carnival-brand cruise travelers visiting the island and the surrounding Caribbean coast.
intro.description: Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal is located in Coxen Hole, on the island of Roatán in the Bay Islands of Honduras. It is a modern cruise terminal serving the beautiful Caribbean coast, providing convenient services and facilities for cruise passengers visiting Roatán and the surrounding Bay Islands.
intro.nearby: When visiting **Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal**, visitors can easily explore surrounding points of interest, including **West Bay Beach** and **West End Village**, two of Roatán's most popular destinations for snorkeling, dining and local culture.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions about Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal
faq.intro: Quick answers to help you plan your visit to Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal:

items.q: Where is Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal located?
items.a: Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal is located in Coxen Hole, on the island of Roatán, in the Bay Islands department of Honduras. Its official address is 8GG3+W27, Coxen Hole, Bay Islands, Honduras.

items.q: Is it free to visit Mahogany Bay?
items.a: Access to the terminal area is free for cruise passengers arriving at the port. Some facilities, such as the Magical Flying Beach Chair, water sports and lounger rentals, may require separate payment.

items.q: Which cruise lines dock at Mahogany Bay?
items.a: The terminal is operated by Carnival Corporation, and its brands, such as Carnival Cruise Line, Holland America Line and Princess Cruises, are the main cruise lines calling at the port.

items.q: How far is the terminal from Roatán's airport?
items.a: Juan Manuel Gálvez International Airport (RTB) is located close to Coxen Hole; the taxi ride from the terminal usually takes about 10-15 minutes.

The terminal only opens on days when cruise ships are in port, and opening times follow the vessels' arrival and departure schedules. Please confirm the day's schedule with your cruise line before traveling.

items.q: How do I get to the beach from the terminal?
items.a: You can take the Magical Flying Beach Chair (chairlift) or walk along the path to Mahogany Bay's beach and shopping village to enjoy the Caribbean sun and sand.

officialManagement.title: About Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal
officialManagement.text: Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal is a modern cruise facility in Coxen Hole, Roatán, Bay Islands, Honduras, owned and managed by Carnival Corporation, serving as a private exclusive gateway to the beautiful Caribbean coast and Roatán Island.

historyTimeline.title: History & Significance of Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal

items.title: Development Period: Terminal Construction
items.description: Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal was developed to accommodate the growing cruise tourism industry in Honduras, providing modern facilities for international cruise passengers.

items.title: Growth Phase: Tourism Expansion
items.description: The terminal experienced significant growth as more cruise lines added Roatán to their itineraries, becoming an important economic driver for the Bay Islands.

items.title: Modern Era: Enhanced Services
items.description: With continuous improvements to facilities and services, the terminal now offers enhanced passenger experience including information services, shopping, and tour arrangements.

items.title: Today: Isla Tropicale & Sustainable Tourism

New amenities — beach clubs, pools and the Mangrove Bay Pool & Swim-Up Bar — are now open to cruise guests, while the terminal continues to balance cruise growth with reef and coastal protection.

historyTimeline.guideContent: When visiting, you can start by **familiarizing yourself with the terminal facilities**; then **visit the information desk** to learn about local attractions; next, **take a shuttle or taxi** to explore the beautiful beaches and coral reefs of Roatán; finally, **return to the terminal** to shop for souvenirs and enjoy local cuisine before departure.

roatan-cruise-ports.metaTitle: Roatán Cruise Ports Compared: Mahogany Bay (Isla Tropicale) vs Port of Roatán
roatan-cruise-ports.metaDescription: Roatán has two separate cruise terminals. Learn the difference between Mahogany Bay (Isla Tropicale) and the Port of Roatán in Coxen Hole — which ships dock where, distances, and how to avoid the wrong port.
roatan-cruise-ports.h1: Roatán Cruise Ports: Mahogany Bay (Isla Tropicale) vs Port of Roatán
roatan-cruise-ports.intro: Roatán has two different cruise terminals, and confusing them is the single most common mistake cruise passengers make. This guide explains the difference between Mahogany Bay — now branded Isla Tropicale — and the Port of Roatán in Coxen Hole, so you arrive at the correct dock.

sections.heading: Two terminals, not one
sections.body: Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal (Isla Tropicale) is Carnival Corporation's private cruise port on the south shore of Roatán, in the Dixon Cove area. The Port of Roatán, sometimes called Coxen Hole Cruise Port, is a separate, publicly run terminal located in Coxen Hole town on the island's north-east side. They are operated by different companies and sit several kilometres apart.

sections.heading: Which ships dock where
sections.body: Mahogany Bay / Isla Tropicale primarily serves Carnival Corporation brands — Carnival Cruise Line, Holland America Line and Princess Cruises. The Port of Roatán in Coxen Hole handles most other lines, including Royal Caribbean, Norwegian, MSC, Celebrity and Disney. Always check your specific ship's itinerary, because the assigned terminal can change.

sections.heading: Distance and location
sections.body: The Port of Roatán is close to Coxen Hole town and about 10–15 minutes from Juan Manuel Gálvez International Airport (RTB). Mahogany Bay / Isla Tropicale is further south in Dixon Cove, roughly 20–30 minutes from the airport depending on traffic. Both are on Roatán but on opposite sides of the island.

sections.heading: Beach and facilities
sections.body: Mahogany Bay has its own private beach (Mahogany Beach), a shopping village, pools, beach clubs and the Magical Flying Beach Chair lift, all inside the gated port. The Port of Roatán has a smaller terminal and no private beach — visitors take a taxi, shuttle or water taxi to West Bay or West End for sand and snorkelling.

sections.heading: How to choose and get between them
sections.body: You don't really choose the terminal — your ship does. If you want to explore beyond your port, taxis and tour operators connect both terminals to West Bay, West End and the rest of the island. If your ship is at Mahogany Bay but you want the town-centre port area, budget about 15–20 minutes of transfer time.

faq.q: Are Mahogany Bay and the Port of Roatán the same place?
faq.a: No. They are two separate cruise terminals on Roatán run by different operators. Mahogany Bay (Isla Tropicale) is Carnival's private port in Dixon Cove; the Port of Roatán is in Coxen Hole town.

faq.q: Which port does Carnival use at Roatán?
faq.a: Carnival Corporation brands — Carnival, Holland America and Princess — dock at Mahogany Bay, now branded Isla Tropicale.

faq.q: Which port does Royal Caribbean, Norwegian or MSC use?
faq.a: These and most other non-Carnival lines typically dock at the Port of Roatán in Coxen Hole, not at Mahogany Bay.

faq.q: How far apart are the two ports?
faq.a: They are on opposite sides of Roatán and are roughly a 15–30 minute drive apart, depending on traffic and exact route.

faq.q: Can I visit Mahogany Bay beach if I dock at Coxen Hole?
faq.a: Yes. Taxis and organised shore excursions can take you from the Port of Roatán to Mahogany Bay and other beaches, but Mahogany Beach amenities are oriented toward cruise guests at that port.

isla-tropicale-roatan.h1: Isla Tropicale Roatán: Carnival's Mahogany Bay Cruise Port
isla-tropicale-roatan.intro: Isla Tropicale is the new name for the Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal, Carnival Corporation's private cruise destination on Roatán's south shore in Dixon Cove. Here is what cruise guests can expect at the refreshed port.

sections.heading: From Mahogany Bay to Isla Tropicale
sections.body: Carnival Corporation rebranded its private Roatán port as Isla Tropicale. The terminal, beach and surrounding facilities are the same physical place — only the name and a set of refreshed amenities are new. You may still see 'Mahogany Bay' on older maps and tickets.

sections.heading: What's at the port
sections.body: Isla Tropicale centres on a Caribbean-style shopping and dining village, Mahogany Beach, swimming pools, beach clubs and the Mangrove Bay Pool & Swim-Up Bar. The atmosphere is a controlled, resort-style cruise destination built for a single day's visit.

sections.heading: The Magical Flying Beach Chair
sections.body: The signature ride is the Magical Flying Beach Chair, an open-air chairlift that carries guests from the shopping village down to Mahogany Beach. It is included for cruise guests and offers a breezy overview of the lagoon and reef.

sections.heading: Getting to the beach
sections.body: From the ship you can ride the Flying Beach Chair or follow the marked walking path to Mahogany Beach. The beach, loungers and lagoon swimming are oriented toward cruise guests; excursions to West Bay or West End leave from the terminal's tour area.

sections.heading: Isla Tropicale vs the rest of Roatán
sections.body: Because Isla Tropicale is a private, gated port, leaving it means booking a taxi, shuttle or organised excursion into Coxen Hole, West Bay or West End. Plan extra transfer time if you want to explore beyond the port's gates.

faq.q: Is Isla Tropicale the same as Mahogany Bay?
faq.a: Yes. Isla Tropicale is the new brand name for the Mahogany Bay Cruise Terminal on Roatán. The location and facilities are the same; the name and some amenities are refreshed.

faq.q: Do I need a ticket to enter Isla Tropicale?
faq.a: No separate ticket is needed — access is included for guests arriving on a Carnival Corporation cruise that calls at the port.

faq.q: Is Mahogany Beach free for cruise guests?
faq.a: Mahogany Beach and its loungers are part of the cruise port experience for guests docking there. Some premium chairs, cabanas, water sports and excursions are paid.

faq.q: What is the Mangrove Bay Pool & Swim-Up Bar?
faq.a: It is one of the refreshed Isla Tropicale amenities — a pool area with a swim-up bar — open to cruise guests at the port.

faq.q: How do I get from Isla Tropicale to West Bay Beach?
faq.a: Taxis, shuttles and organised shore excursions run from the terminal's tour area to West Bay and West End; budget roughly 30–40 minutes each way.
